parts: Lesson 14: Growth and Patterns of Tourism in World — Summary

Growth means the increase or decrease in the number of tourists compared with an earlier period (negative growth if fewer); pattern means the spatial distribution of tourism over the earth. Factors affecting world tourism: high income of the tourist (per capita income is the best guide), paid holidays or holiday entitlement, travel cost (low to moderate cost boosts tourism), technology (information on the internet), package providers and tour operators, media and updated knowledge, a growing middle class in developing countries and the rise of new destinations with more tourism investment.

Cultural (historical and archaeological sites, architecture, monuments, museums, performing arts, cuisine), natural (landscapes, seascapes, mountains, islands, beaches, parks, flora and fauna, caves), events (mega-events, trade fairs, conferences, community events, festivals, religious events such as the Haj and the Maha Kumbh, sports events such as the Olympics, football and cricket world cups), recreational (sightseeing, golf, swimming, tennis, cricket, snow sports, mountaineering, rafting) and entertainment (theme and amusement parks, casinos, shopping, sports complexes). Spatial distribution depends on natural landscape, beautiful sites, accessibility and moderate climate plus man-made beautification; tourism is concentrated in Europe, around the Mediterranean and in the USA, and growing in developing countries.

UNWTO (headquarters at Madrid, Spain) reported that in 2015 France was the top destination (about 67.3 million arrivals as listed in the lesson), then the USA, Spain, Italy, UK, China, Poland, Mexico, Canada and Hungary. World arrivals: 983 million (2011), 1,035 million (2012), 1,087 million (2013), 1,135 million (2014, up 4.3–4.4%) and 1,184 million (2015, up 4.4%), the sixth consecutive year of above-average growth; expected growth about 4% a year. From 530 million in 1995 arrivals nearly doubled to 1,035 million in 2012, crossing a billion for the first time; in 2012 Asia and the Pacific recorded the highest growth (7%). Growth was mainly in East Asia and the Pacific (about 13% a year) and the Middle East (10%). Europe and the Americas held 95% of arrivals in 1950, 82% in 1990 and 76% in 2000.

Share of arrivals in 2015: Europe 609 million (51%), Asia and Pacific 278 million (23%), Americas 191 million, Middle East 54 million and Africa 53 million (5%, the minimum). Tourist arrivals are the persons who arrive at a tourist centre and stay at least a night, counted without any age limit. International tourist receipts are all expenditure by inbound visitors (accommodation, transport, food, entertainment, souvenirs, entry fees). Receipts reached US$ 1,245 billion in 2014 (up 3.7% in real terms), Europe having the largest share (41%), then Asia and the Pacific (30%), the Americas (22%), the Middle East (4%) and Africa (3%). Total exports from international tourism were US$ 1.5 trillion, about US$ 4 billion a day.

Growth outside the developed world became noticeable from 1970. The average world growth is about 4–4.5% a year. By 2020 Europe is projected to have about 717 million tourists (3.1% growth); East Asia and the Pacific to grow 6.5% a year with 25% share (replacing the Americas as second); Africa and the Middle East over 7% and South Asia to reach about 19 million tourists. World Tourism Day is celebrated on 27 September to foster awareness of the importance of tourism.
